stances.claim: The Constitution and the Rules of Court establish a clear bail framework: everyone has a right to bail except those charged with capital offenses when evidence of guilt is strong -- and the strength-of-evidence determination is a factual matter committed to the sound discretion of the trial court, exercised only after a four-step procedural sequence (hearing, prosecution notice, accused's chance to counter, summary determination).

Enrile v. Sandiganbayan (Aug 18, 2015) established that bail may also be granted on 'special humanitarian grounds' -- citing advanced age (91 at the time), ill health (uncontrolled hypertension, arrhythmia, coronary calcification, ACOS exacerbations), 'social and political standing,' and 'immediate surrender to the authorities.'

The Supreme Court correctly remanded the matter to the trial court -- but, 'with due respect, it took too unreasonably long to act': the petition was filed in April, the Court acted only on July 28, and announced its action only on September 10. It should have 'immediately dismissed the facially defective petition outright' (per CJ's Sept 27 column 'Dismissed on short shrift').

Part of the fault also lies with Nasino's lawyers, who went to the Supreme Court too soon -- they should have insisted on the trial court setting a bail hearing first and gone to the SC only to contest a trial-court denial rendered with grave abuse of discretion.

Strictly speaking, the Enrile 'humanitarian grounds' do not extend by direct application to Nasino because Enrile's grounds referred to the accused while Nasino's grounds referred to the baby, not the mother.

Nonetheless, CJ endorses Naga RTC Judge Soliman M. Santos Jr.'s liberal approach: bail could have been granted by analogy under Article 3 of the 1989 Convention on the Rights of the Child ('the best interests of the child shall be a primary consideration') -- operationalized through the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006's definition of 'best interest of the child' as 'the totality of circumstances and conditions which are most congenial to the survival, protection and feelings of security of the child and most encouraging to the child's physical, psychological and emotional development.'

Looking forward, the SC and/or Congress should respond to the public outrage by 'studying and possibly codifying new rules and/or new laws to protect the unborn and the young children of detained mothers.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban responds to the Inquirer's October 29 editorial decrying the 'egregious failure of the justice system that led to the death of baby River Nasino after she was separated from her mother,' detainee Reina Mae Nasino. He sets out a five-step bail framework: (1) Constitution Article III Section 13 -- everyone has a right to bail except those charged with capital offenses when evidence of guilt is strong; (2) Rules of Court Section 7 Rule 114 repeats the rule negatively; (3) the strength-of-evidence question is a factual matter committed to the sound discretion of the trial court, exercised only after a four-step procedure (hearing, prosecution notice, accused's chance to counter, summary determination); (4) the intent is to assure appearance and minimize flight risk; and (5) Enrile v. Sandiganbayan (August 18, 2015) added 'special humanitarian grounds' -- citing advanced age (91), ill health (uncontrolled hypertension, arrhythmia, coronary calcification, ACOS exacerbations), 'social and political standing,' and 'immediate surrender to the authorities.' CJ believes the Supreme Court correctly remanded the matter to the trial court but, 'with due respect, it took too unreasonably long to act' -- the petition was filed in April, the Court acted only on July 28, and announced its action only on September 10. It should have dismissed the facially defective petition outright (per CJ's September 27, 2020 column 'Dismissed on short shrift'). Part of the fault lies with Nasino's lawyers, who went to the SC too soon rather than first insisting on a trial-court bail hearing. Post-remand, the trial court was 'unduly strict' -- it 'mindlessly denied the petition for hospital stay and needlessly separated the baby from her detained mother, to quote again the Inquirer editorial, to tragic results.' Strictly speaking, the Enrile humanitarian grounds do not extend to Nasino because those referred to the accused while Nasino's referred to the baby, not the mother. Nonetheless, CJ endorses the liberal approach proposed by Naga RTC Judge Soliman M. Santos Jr. in an email: bail could have been granted by analogy under Article 3 of the 1989 Convention on the Rights of the Child ('the best interests of the child shall be a primary consideration'), operationalized via the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006's definition of 'best interest of the child' as 'the totality of circumstances and conditions which are most congenial to the survival, protection and feelings of security of the child and most encouraging to the child's physical, psychological and emotional development.' He closes with a hope that 'the Supreme Court and/or Congress will respond to the public outrage by studying and possibly codifying new rules and/or new laws to protect the unborn and the young children of detained mothers.'
